question: Which song by The Beatles starts with a chord jump from the tonic to the minor fitfh chord?

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The textbook example is *Helter Skelter*.

The song is in E major. The very first two harmonic statements are the tonic E major and then a jump up a perfect fifth to the v chord, B minor. In the familiar studio intro the E major power-chord/harmony is stated and is immediately answered by the B minor / B5 harmony, i.e. I → v, the tonic to the minor fifth degree of the key. The I–v jump is what gives the number its characteristic heavy, open fifth-leap feel and is the Beatles’ most quoted I-to-minor-v opening.

5.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I’d go with “A Day in the Life”. The opening is that famous held G major tonic — the piano really sits on G for a few bars — and then it makes that characteristic big leap up a tritone to the D♭ major / minor fifth harmony before the first vocal line lands. It’s a dramatic tonic-to-♭5 jump that sets up the whole suite-like opening, and it’s the jump most people remember as the song’s signature entrance.

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I’m going to go with Penny Lane.

The intro is the giveaway. It’s often talked about as the paired side with Strawberry Fields Forever, and both sit in that late-’66/early-’67 psychedelic space where The Beatles were really leaning on a tritone opening. Penny Lane is set up in D major for the verses, and the very first hit of the piccolo trumpet fanfare / piano intro lands on the D tonic and then immediately leaps to the G♭ major chord – the minor fifth / tritone of D – before the melody settles in. That D → G♭ jump is the same kind of tonic-to-minor-fifth shock you hear talked about for those era openers, and it’s what makes the opening of Penny Lane sound so disorienting and bright at the same time. The jump sets up the whole A-section’s harmonic colour and is the reason the introduction is usually described as a tritone displacement from the home key.

That E → B♭ leap is the jarring, almost blues-rock tritone jump that defines the intro before the riff settles, and it’s the kind of dramatic tonic-to-flat-five interval the question is describing.

9.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Penny Lane. The opening is a classic tonic-to-v jump. The piccolo trumpet intro establishes the tonic, B♭ major, and when the full band comes in the first guitar/bass hit lands on F minor, the minor v chord a perfect fifth up from the tonic. That F minor to B♭ back-and-forth is what gives the intro its unsettled, slightly sour lift right at the start, and it’s usually described as the tonic jumping straight to the minor fifth before settling into the verse groove.

3.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The classic tritone / tonic – flat-five opening that is
quoted in Beatles harmonic studies is the one that opens *Come
Together* / the *Walrus / Day in the Life* family of openings.

In the most often cited reading the song is heard in E, the
intro riff is heard as an E tonic sonority which is immediately
answered by a sonority a tritone / a minor 5th away, the ♭V /
v material that underlies the famous “Come Together” riff and
that is the textbook I – bV / I – v jump that is quoted for
*I Am the Walrus* / *A Day in the Life* in the literature.  In
concert keys the move is often described as C → G♭ , i.e. a tonic
major triad followed immediately by the chord a minor fifth /
tritone away, the flattened fifth/minor-fifth chord that gives
the opening its characteristic harsh lift. That is the I → ♭V
tonic-to-minor-fifth jump that is normally illustrated with the
*Come Together / Walrus* opening.

8.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The textbook example that is normally quoted is the string
intro of the 1966 *Revolver* track Eleanor Rigby. 

The piece is in D natural minor and the first two sounding harmonies of the
8‑part string octet are

    i   –   v

D minor  →  A minor

i.e. the tonic triad D–F–A is stated and then jumped a perfect 5th up to the
minor‑quality dominant, the v chord A–C–E, the minor fifth / the 5th degree
made minor, of the key. In the published lead‑sheet it is the D–m // A–m
opening that launches the “Ah, look at all the lonely people” ostinato and
is the move that is usually quoted as the Beatles’ I→v tonic-to-minor-fifth
launch. 

The same I→v  move is the one most often pointed to, in the major‑mode
literature, with the opening of I Saw Her Standing There/A Hard Day’s Night
type material, A major → E minor – the tonic of the key jumped a fifth to the
minor fifth degree E minor. That is the formal equivalent of the D–m/A–m i–v
opening that everyone cites for Eleanor Rigby.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: The textbook example that is normally quoted is the opening of
A Day in the Life / I Am The Walrus family of openings.

The well known Beatles tritone / I–♭V opening is the one that is quoted for
A Day in the Life and in the same family for I Am The Walrus.  In the common
A-major reading of the introduction the music sits on the tonic A major for

that is the usual “Beatles tritone opening” that is cited in the literature,
and it is the same kind of I → ♭V jump that is made explicit on the opening
piano riff of I Am The Walrus, c. C → G♭, the classic Beatles tonic-to-flat-five
opening.

11.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I Saw Her Standing There

The iconic opening of the 1963 A Hard Day’s Night / Please Please Me material is the
A major → E minor figure that John plays on the opening “She was just 17…” 
verse. 

In A major the diatonic 5th degree is E major. The Beatles voice the 5th
degree in its parallel-minor form, E minor, v, and put it right up against the
tonic. The song therefore opens with the very audible tonic-to-minor-fifth
jump A – E m, tonic to v, and then settles into the I–V–vi–IV-type rock
and roll that follows. That I–v opening is the one most often cited as the
Beatles’ textbook tonic-to-minor-fifth jump; the same I–v gesture is heard in
the same spirit at the famous E–B m launch of Helter Skelter/ No Reply, C–G m
in No Reply etc.

The famous tritone jump that is quoted in Beatles analysis is the
opening of the Revolver/White-Album period.

The piece that is normally quoted is **“I Am The Walrus”**. In the A-major
section that opens the song the piano first hits the tonic A – A–C♯–E – and
is answered immediately by the tritone/flat-five substitute E♭ – G♭ – B♭,
i.e. the chord a minor 5th / diminished 5th – a tritone – away from the
tonic. The A–E♭ leap, A → E♭, is the I → bV / I → ♭5 tritone jump that is
usually described as the tonic to the minor-fifth chord. It is the same
kind of I→♭V opening that is also spoken of for the first piano statement
of *A Day in the Life*, the A-major tonic piano chord that is answered by
the E♭-major tritone/flat-five colour before the song settles into its
A-major verse. That tritone I–♭V opening is the Beatles’ classic
tonic-to-minor-fifth jump.

i  →  v

commonly referred to in the literature on the Beatles’ early-’67 minor

* I Saw Her Standing There: cited as A major → E minor, I → v, the A–Em launch of the Please Please Me / A Hard Day’s Night era material.
* Strawberry Fields Forever / Norwegian Wood family: often described as A major → E minor, the same I → v colour.
* No Reply: C major → G minor, I → v.

* Yer Blues: E minor → B minor, i → v.
* Eleanor Rigby: D minor → A minor, i → v, the string-octet opening often quoted as the textbook i → v launch.

A Hard Day’s Night is repeatedly mentioned by colleagues 10, 15, etc. as G → E minor. In G major E is the 6th degree, vi, not the fifth degree v = D. Current weight: the most consistently cited major-mode I → v textbook illustration in the thread is Helter Skelter E → Bm, with I Saw Her Standing There A → Em as a closely competing early-Beatles example. Yer Blues/Eleanor Rigby are valid i → v instances but are minor-mode.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the Walrus is the one that actually fits the wording if you take “minor fifth” literally as the flattened fifth/tritone.

Strawberry Fields Forever, Helter Skelter, A Hard Day’s Night, I Saw Her Standing There and the whole I → v family all do a tonic to the *diatonic* fifth degree made minor. That’s E major → B minor, A major → E minor, G major → E minor, etc. It’s a perfect fifth in the bass, the v chord, and it’s the opening everyone is talking about in the White Album/’67 literature. That’s a tonic to a perfect fifth, not a minor fifth.

The jump the question is describing is the tonic to a chord a diminished/minor fifth away, i.e. a tritone/b♭V. That’s the famous Beatles “wrong” opening and it’s the one that’s repeatedly taught as the tonic-to-♭5 jump.

I Am the Walrus is the textbook example of that. The intro is set up as a tonic statement and then an immediate tritone displacement. In the commonly cited reading it’s F major → C♯m, essentially F → bV, and in the A-major section it’s A → E♭. Colleagues 16, 19 and 20 are pointing at exactly that A → E♭ and C → G♭ type move. That’s the interval that gives the Walrus its famously unsettled, off-kilter entrance before it settles into the verse, and it’s the same family of tonic-to-tritone openings that people associate with A Day in the Life and Come Together.

Penny Lane is close in spirit and is often paired with Strawberry Fields in the Magical Mystery Tour era, but the Strawberry Fields argument itself is messy: the released single is the splice of two takes in different keys/tempos, and the “E major → B minor” / “A major → E minor” story is a perfect-fifth v motion, not a minor-fifth/tritone motion. Once you separate the perfect-fifth v openings from the actual tritone b♭V openings, Walrus is the clean, unanimous teaching example for a tonic-to-minor-fifth / tonic-to-tritone jump.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the late-66 single pair is exactly what’s causing the mix-up here, and Colleague 18 and Colleague 12 have put their finger on why.

The A – E m I → v move is absolutely the textbook move that gets quoted for Strawberry Fields Forever, and it’s the reason the song is always mentioned in this family alongside Penny Lane and Norwegian Wood. That is the canonical “tonic to the minor fifth degree” citation in the literature.

Where I keep coming back to Penny Lane is that it’s the cleanest, most unambiguously audible studio realization of that gesture from that same release. The piccolo-trumpet fanfare is universally described as establishing the home tonic, and the first full band hit that follows the fanfare is the jarring lift a fifth/tritone away from it – the chord that writers routinely label as the minor-fifth / flattened-fifth colour. Strawberry Fields Forever is often misremembered for that jump because the two singles were released together and share the same harmonic language, and the Strawberry Fields intro itself is a blended tape-loop / vocal entry that’s much less cleanly tonic-defined than Penny Lane’s brass-led statement. Once you separate the pair, Penny Lane is the one you can point to in 10 seconds and hear the tonic → minor-fifth intervallic launch with no ambiguity about tape effects or modal mixture. If we keep the definition strict in the way it is used in Beatles harmony writing, it is
I → v, i.e. tonic root moved a perfect 5th up to the triad built on the 5th degree
voiced in its minor quality. That is a root movement P5, not a tritone, and it is the
v / i–v fifth-leap that the Beatles return to again and again at an opening.

On that strict reading the textbook example is the White Album E major/minor
launch. The studio intro of Helter Skelter is entered on a big E major
tonic sonority and the first harmonic answer is the v chord, B minor,
E → Bm, I → v. The same I → v gesture is the one that is repeatedly quoted
for the A major version of the early rock & roll riff family,
A → Em in I Saw Her Standing There / the Strawberry Fields Forever
A major/minor intro, and it is the i → v analogue that is actually bar-accurate
in the string octet of Eleanor Rigby, Dm → Am i → v, and in Yer Blues,
Em → Bm i → v.

That is the I / i to minor-quality fifth-degree opening that is normally described
as the Beatles’ “tonic-to-minor-fifth” jump.

The tritone I → ♭V / I → b5 family that a lot of colleagues are citing for Penny
Lane, I Am the Walrus and A Day in the Life is a different interval class: a

Once the interval class is pinned to a perfect-fifth root move to a minor quality
fifth degree, Helter Skelter’s E major → B minor I → v launch, and the

I think the Walrus is the one that actually fits the wording if you take “minor fifth” literally as the flattened fifth/tritone.

Strawberry Fields Forever, Helter Skelter, A Hard Day’s Night, I Saw Her Standing There and the whole I → v family all do a tonic to the *diatonic* fifth degree made minor. That is the diatonic tonic-to-minor-fifth-degree opening that is normally described as the Beatles’ canonical I → v jump. 

If the question is being read strictly as a literal tritone / ♭V jump, i.e. tonic to a chord a diminished 5th/minor 5th interval away, the family that is quoted for that is the *A Day in the Life / I Am the Walrus* group, e.g. G → D♭ / A → E♭ / C → G♭, I → ♭V, which is a different formal description from the I → v fifth-degree minor colour above.
public_text.17:
I think Penny Lane is the one that actually fits the description cleanly, and it’s the example that keeps coming up once you listen to the first few bars without the mythology around it.

The intro is set up as B♭ major. The piccolo trumpet fanfare lands unambiguously on the tonic B♭ and the band’s first full-band hit under the vocal entrance is F minor, the v chord, the minor triad built on the 5th degree of B♭ major. That is a textbook tonic → v, tonic to the minor fifth-degree chord, perfect-fifth jump up from the tonic, and it’s why the opening has that slightly unsettled, almost music-hall lift before it settles into the verse groove.

It’s often described as a tritone because of how brightly the piccolo sits against the harmony, and that’s probably why it gets conflated with the Strawberry Fields/Norwegian Wood family. Strawberry Fields is frequently quoted for the same gesture, but the fade-in and the double-tracked / ADT vocal make the tonic identification much less immediate in the studio version. The first clearly diatonic pair you can actually notate reliably is in a different key area than the A – E m reading that gets repeated, and the intro is layered enough that people remember the “jump” more as a colour than as a clean I → v statement.

Penny Lane gives you the clean I → v launch right at the start, tonic B♭ major straight to F minor v, with no fade and no ambiguity about which sonority is the home key. That’s the tonic-to-minor-fifth opening that the Beatles keep returning to in the late ’66/early ’67 period.

Helter Skelter

In the conventional major-mode reading the opening is the textbook I → v perfect-fifth root move.

The number is set up in E major. The first harmonic statement in the studio intro is a full E major tonic sonority and it is answered immediately by the v chord a perfect fifth up, B minor / B5. E → Bm is tonic to the minor-quality 5th degree of the key, I → v, the classic heavy open-fifth launch that gives the track its instantly recognisable jump.

The same I → v gesture is what is quoted in the early Beatles literature for the A major → E minor launch of I Saw Her Standing There / the Strawberry Fields / Norwegian Wood family, and in minor-mode form i → v as in Yer Blues Em → Bm and Eleanor Rigby Dm → Am. Helter Skelter is the major-mode I → v example that is most consistently cited in the literature as the canonical tonic-to-minor-fifth opening, distinct from the tritone I → ♭V / I → bV jumps that are being discussed for Penny Lane, I Am the Walrus, A Day in the Life and Come Together.

I think the late-66 single pair is exactly what’s causing the mix-up here, and Colleague 18 and Colleague 12 have put their finger on why.

The A – E m I → v move is absolutely the textbook move that gets quoted for Strawberry Fields Forever, and it’s the reason the song is always mentioned in this family alongside Penny Lane and Norwegian Wood. That is the canonical “tonic to the minor fifth degree” citation in the literature.

Where I keep coming back to Penny Lane is that it’s the cleanest, most unambiguously audible studio realization of that gesture from that same release. The piccolo-trumpet fanfare is universally described as establishing the home tonic, and the first full band hit that follows the fanfare is the jarring lift a fifth/tritone away from it – the chord that writers routinely label as the minor-fifth / flattened-fifth colour. It’s the jolt that gives the intro its carnival-unsettled quality before the verse settles in, and it’s the example most people actually hear first when they think of the Magical Mystery Tour / Strawberry Fields era opening.

Strawberry Fields Forever is often misremembered for that jump because the two singles were released together and share the same harmonic language, and the Strawberry Fields intro itself is a blended tape-loop / vocal entry that’s much less cleanly tonic-defined than Penny Lane’s brass-led statement. Once you separate the pair, Penny Lane is the one you can point to in 10 seconds and hear the tonic → minor-fifth intervallic launch with no ambiguity about tape effects or modal mixture. That’s why the “tonic to minor fifth” description keeps getting attached to Penny Lane in practice.

The split in round 0 is really a split over what “minor fifth chord” is being meant.

If we keep the definition strict in the way it is used in Beatles harmony writing, it is
I → v, i.e. tonic root moved a perfect 5th up to the triad built on the 5th degree
voiced in its minor quality. That is a root movement P5, not a tritone, and it is the
v / i–v fifth-leap that the Beatles return to again and again at an opening.

On that strict reading the textbook example is the White Album E major/minor
launch. The studio intro of Helter Skelter is entered on a big E major
tonic sonority and the first harmonic answer is the v chord, B minor,
E → Bm, I → v. The same I → v gesture is the one that is repeatedly quoted
for the A major version of the early rock & roll riff family,
A → Em in I Saw Her Standing There / the Strawberry Fields Forever
A major/minor intro, and it is the i → v analogue that is actually bar-accurate
in the string octet of Eleanor Rigby, Dm → Am i → v, and in Yer Blues,
Em → Bm i → v.

That is the I / i to minor-quality fifth-degree opening that is normally described
as the Beatles’ “tonic-to-minor-fifth” jump.

The tritone I → ♭V / I → b5 family that a lot of colleagues are citing for Penny
Lane, I Am the Walrus and A Day in the Life is a different interval class: a
root movement of a diminished 5th / augmented 4th, e.g. the often-quoted
G → E♭ / A → E♭ / F → C♯m openings. That is a tonic-to-flat-five tritone
displacement, not a tonic-to-the-minor-quality-fifth-degree v.

Once the interval class is pinned to a perfect-fifth root move to a minor quality
fifth degree, Helter Skelter’s E major → B minor I → v launch, and the
literally verifiable i → v launches Dm → Am in Eleanor Rigby and Em → Bm in
Yer Blues, are the canonical realizations. Helter Skelter is the one most
repeatedly quoted in the literature for the major-mode I → v textbook case.

reflection_text.4:
The deliberation remains split on the definition of “minor fifth chord”. One camp reads it as the diatonic 5th-degree chord in minor quality, i.e. I → v / i → v with a perfect-fifth root movement; the other camp reads it literally as a chord a minor-fifth/tritone interval away from the tonic, i.e. I → ♭V.

I → v perfect-fifth family, repeatedly reaffirmed in round 1:
* Helter Skelter E major → B minor I → v is the most-quoted major-mode textbook instance, Colleagues 1,10,11,19,3,8,19,3,8. 
* A Hard Day’s Night G major → E minor and I Saw Her Standing There A major → E minor are presented as the archetype of the same I → v fifth-degree-minor launch, Colleagues 12,15,20,4,6. The G→Em/A→Em riff is the canonical pop-theory citation for the move.
* Minor-mode analogues are consistently noted: Yer Blues E minor → B minor i → v, Colleague 12; Eleanor Rigby D minor → A minor i → v, Colleagues 8,18. Strawberry Fields Forever / Norwegian Wood are described as the same class, E/A → Bm / Em → Bm I→v.

Penny Lane is the main contested node:
* Colleagues 13,14,17,9 argue for a clean I → v perfect-fifth reading: Bb major → F minor v, tonic to the minor-quality fifth degree, with the piccolo fanfare establishing Bb and the first full band hit being Fm.
* Colleagues 2,16,21 argue Penny Lane is the tritone/flat-five example, D major → Gb major or the same gesture described as Bb → Gb, i.e. I → ♭V, pairing it with the Magical Mystery Tour/Strawberry Fields era.

Tritone I → ♭V family:
* I Am The Walrus / A Day In The Life are consistently cited for a true minor-fifth/tritone jump: F → C♯m / A → E♭ / C → G♭, I → ♭V. Colleagues 5,6,7,19,20,7,5.
* Penny Lane and Come Together are also placed in this family by several contributors.

Errors / corrections noticed:
* Frequent key mis-identifications for Penny Lane and Strawberry Fields. Strawberry Fields is A→Em / E→Bm I→v, not a tritone.
* Conflation of perfect-fifth root movement to a minor-quality v chord with a diminished-fifth root movement to a ♭V chord. The wording “minor fifth chord” is used for both.
* Some contributors describe Helter Skelter as a tritone E→B♭, which is inconsistent with the standard E→Bm analysis.

Current best working understanding:
The textbook Beatles I → v tonic-to-minor-fifth-degree opening is the A Hard Day’s Night / I Saw Her Standing There family, G→Em / A→Em, with Helter Skelter E→Bm as the most repeatedly cited major-mode instance. Yer Blues Em→Bm and Eleanor Rigby Dm→Am are verifiable i→v analogues. The Penny Lane / Walrus / A Day In The Life citations belong to the separate I→♭V tritone family. Unresolved is which reading the question intends: diatonic v vs literal tritone. If literal minor-fifth interval is required, the canonical teaching example is the Walrus/A Day In The Life I→♭V tritone opening, with Penny Lane often paired in discussion.

I am keeping both families in mind. reflection_text.1:
The terminological split from round 0 persists in round 1 and is now more explicit.

*I → v / i → v = tonic root moved a perfect fifth to the 5th degree made minor*
Proponents remain the majority of the I → v camp:
* Helter Skelter E major → B minor I → v is repeatedly called the textbook major-mode example. Colleague 1,10,11,19,3,8 cite E → Bm as the canonical heavy open-fifth launch, with the same gesture also named for I Saw Her Standing There A major → E minor / No Reply and for the A Hard Day’s Night/G major → E minor family.
* The minor-mode analogues are consistently listed: Yer Blues E minor → B minor i → v, Eleanor Rigby D minor → A minor i → v, Strawberry Fields Forever E major/minor → B minor / A major → E minor.
* A Hard Day’s Night / I Saw Her Standing There is still the most popularly named archetype, with Colleague 12,15,20,6,4 calling G major → E minor / A major → E minor the canonical I → v launch. Note the music-theory error that keeps surfacing: G → E is a minor third / major sixth root movement, not a perfect fifth; the diatonic fifth degree of G is D, so the correct diatonic v is D minor. The E minor reading is the one the literature actually uses for that riff, so the interval description is sloppy.
* Penny Lane is now being fought over. Colleague 13,14,17,9 argue it is the clean I → v perfect-fifth example: B♭ major → F minor v, a perfect fifth up, the “carnival-unsettled” lift that is paired with Strawberry Fields. Colleague 16,2,21 and earlier tritone proponents still hear it as a tritone/flat-five launch, usually rendered D major → G♭ major or B♭ → F/G♭, i.e. I → ♭V.

*I → ♭V / tritone = tonic to a chord a minor fifth / diminished fifth interval away*
This camp remains strong:
* I Am the Walrus is the most consistently named tritone example: F → C♯m, A → E♭, C → G♭, D → A♭ depending on the transcription, with Colleague 16,19,20,5,7 calling it the textbook tonic-to-tritone / tonic-to-♭V jump.
* A Day in the Life is cited as the classic G major → D♭ major / A major → E♭ major I → ♭V opening, Colleague 5,6,20.
* Penny Lane is also claimed here as D → G♭ tritone, Colleague 2,16.
* Come Together is added to the Walrus/Day in the Life family, Colleague 3.

Errors / corrections noticed:
* Conflation of perfect-fifth root movement I → v with tritone I → ♭V persists. Helter Skelter is simultaneously claimed as E → Bm I → v and E → B♭ tritone by Colleague 7.
* Penny Lane is claimed both as B♭ → Fm I → v and as D → G♭ I → ♭V; the two statements are mutually exclusive.
* Several colleagues still describe A Hard Day’s Night as G → E minor as a “perfect fifth” move, which is intervallically inaccurate.
* I Am the Walrus is rendered in multiple keys F/C/A/D across colleagues, but the functional description I → ♭V is stable.

What remains solid:
* The Beatles do use a tonic → minor-quality fifth-degree opening repeatedly, e.g. A → Em, E → Bm, Em → Bm, Dm → Am.
* The White Album/Revolver era also uses i → v as above.
* The tritone I → ♭V opening is a separate later trope exemplified by A Day in the Life / I Am the Walrus / Penny Lane in the tritone reading.

Unresolved:
* Whether the question intends I → v perfect-fifth root movement to a minor-quality fifth degree, or a literal minor-fifth interval = tritone I → ♭V.
* Which track is the most canonical single example under the intended definition. Under the I → v reading the strongest consistently repeated textbook citation is Helter Skelter E → Bm, with A Hard Day’s Night / I Saw Her Standing There A → Em as the popularly named equivalent. Under the literal minor-fifth/tritone reading the literature points to I Am the Walrus / A Day in the Life, with Penny Lane D → G♭ being the disputed Magical Mystery Tour instance.

Current leaning: the question is still ambiguous. If it means the textbook pop-theory “tonic to the minor fifth degree” = I → v, the consensus example is Helter Skelter E major → B minor, with I Saw Her Standing There / A Hard Day’s Night as the same gesture in A/G. If it means a literal chord a minor fifth / tritone away from the tonic = I → ♭V, the canonical teaching example is I Am the Walrus / A Day in the Life, with Penny Lane often paired. Need clarification of “minor fifth chord” meaning.

Evidence strongest for the diatonic v reading is the unanimous teaching literature around A Hard Day’s Night / I Saw Her Standing There G → Em / A → Em and Helter Skelter E → Bm, with verifiable i → v openings in Eleanor Rigby and Yer Blues. The core ambiguity that is driving the round-1 split is what “minor fifth chord’’ means.

Interpretation A – the one most colleagues use in the I → v literature – is root movement a perfect fifth from tonic to the triad built on the 5th scale degree voiced minor, i.e. I → v in major and i → v in minor. That is a perfect-fifth root jump to a minor-quality fifth-degree chord, not a tritone.

On that reading the canonical major-mode textbook examples are:
* Helter Skelter, studio intro in E major/minor: E major → B minor, I → v. This is the most repeatedly quoted major-mode I → v launch and the one I have been keeping as the lead candidate.
* I Saw Her Standing There, A major → E minor, I → v. The same gesture, historically earlier, and routinely cited alongside Helter Skelter/No Reply.
* Minor-mode equivalents: Yer Blues E minor i → B minor v and Eleanor Rigby string octet D minor i → A minor v, i → v perfect-fifth launches that are bar-accurate.
* Penny Lane is now being advanced by several colleagues as B♭ major → F minor, i.e. I → v, a perfect-fifth tonic-to-minor-fifth-degree jump. The same song is also claimed by the tritone camp as D/B♭ → G♭, illustrating how much the key identification drives the disagreement.

Interpretation B – tonic to a chord a minor-fifth/tritone interval away, i.e. I → ♭V – is a different interval class. The colleagues in this camp cite:
* I Am The Walrus, often read as F → C♯m / A → E♭, the classic “wrong” tritone entrance.
* A Day in the Life, the A → E♭ / G → D♭ tonic-to-flat-five opening.
* Penny Lane in the D major → G♭ major reading and Come Together / Penny Lane-style tritone displacements.

Errors / corrections noted in round 1:
* The G major → E minor = v claim for A Hard Day’s Night is musically inaccurate on a diatonic reading. In G major E minor is the vi degree, not the v degree; the fifth degree of G is D. The G → E minor colour is a VI/mediant move, not I → v. The same inaccuracy infects several A Hard Day’s Night citations. The A major → E minor form in I Saw Her Standing There remains correct for I → v.
* The confusion between a perfect-fifth root move to a minor-quality v chord and a tritone root move to a ♭V chord is systematic. Many colleagues conflate the two under the loose phrase “tonic to minor fifth”.

Changes in my own weighting:
* Helter Skelter stays the strongest, most repeatedly quoted major-mode I → v textbook example, with I Saw Her Standing There A → Em as the historically early equivalent and Eleanor Rigby Dm → Am / Yer Blues Em → Bm as the clear minor-mode i → v analogues.
* Penny Lane is now a live contender for the I → v reading under the B♭ → Fm analysis, but the key/analysis dispute means it cannot be taken as settled.
* If the question is literally intended as a tonic-to-chord-a-minor-fifth-interval-away, i.e. I → ♭V/tritone, then the Walrus / A Day in the Life family is the correct formal class, distinct from the I → v perfect-fifth family above.

Unresolved:
* The question writer’s intended definition of “minor fifth chord”. Does it mean “chord on the fifth degree made minor” or “chord a minor fifth/tritone away from tonic”? The deliberation is split roughly along that line.

I am retaining Helter Skelter as the lead I → v answer, with I Saw Her Standing There / Eleanor Rigby / Yer Blues as corroborating I → v examples, while keeping the tritone I → ♭V camp – Walrus / A Day in the Life and the Penny Lane tritone reading – as the alternative interpretation if “minor fifth’’ is read as an interval rather than a scale degree.

On that conventional diatonic-v reading the major-mode canonical statement is the White Album intro

* Helter Skelter – studio intro in E major/minor

E major / E5 → B minor / B5

E → Bm is I → v. The tonic is stated as a full open E major power chord and the first harmonic answer is the minor-quality fifth-degree chord a perfect fifth up, B minor / B5. That is the heavy open-fifth tonic-to-minor-fifth-degree launch that is routinely quoted alongside the early-rock-and-roll prototype

* I Saw Her Standing There A major → E minor I → v
* A Hard Day’s Night G major → E minor I → v

and the minor-mode bar-accurate analogues

* Yer Blues E minor → B minor i → v
* Eleanor Rigby D minor → A minor i → v in the string octet.

Helter Skelter E → Bm is the major-mode instantiation that is most repeatedly cited as the clean, unambiguously notatable studio realisation of the gesture. Strawberry Fields Forever is in the same I → v family, A → Em / E → Bm, but the released single is a fade-in with ADT vocal and a splice of two takes in different keys/tempos, so the tonic is less immediately defined at bar one than in Helter Skelter.

That is distinct from the literal interval reading tonic to a chord a diminished fifth / tritone away, I → ♭V. On the literal I → ♭V / flat-five reading the late-66/67 tritone family is I Am the Walrus / A Day in the Life, F → C♯m / A → E♭ / G → D♭ / C → G♭, with Penny Lane being the clean audible Magical Mystery Tour example that is quoted both as B♭ → Fm I → v in the standard diatonic reading and as D → G♭ / B♭ → G♭ I → ♭V in the literal interval reading.

I think we need to pin down what “minor fifth chord” means in the wording of the question, because that’s where the Strawberry Fields / Penny Lane confusion is being generated.

If we take the phrase literally, a chord a minor fifth away from the tonic is a tritone / flat-five displacement, I → ♭V, an intervallic minor fifth in pitch space, not a perfect-fifth root move to a minor-quality diatonic v chord. That is a different interval class from the I → v perfect-fifth-to-minor-quality-fifth-degree launch that the literature normally describes as “tonic to the minor fifth degree”.

Strawberry Fields Forever is the textbook example of the second class, not the first. The move that is quoted for it is A major → E minor, and in the E reading that gets carried into the White Album material E major → B minor. That is a root movement of a perfect fifth from tonic to the triad built on the fifth degree made minor, I → v. It is the same formal family as Helter Skelter E → Bm, A Hard Day’s Night G → Em, I Saw Her Standing There A → Em, and the i → v examples in Yer Blues and Eleanor Rigby. It is a perfect-fifth in the bass to a minor-quality v chord, not a chord a minor-fifth / tritone interval away from the tonic.

The studio realisation reinforces that. The released single is a fade-in with ADT vocal and the famous two-take splice in different keys and tempos. The tonic is never stated as a clean block chord at bar one; the harmony emerges out of the fade and the double-tracked vocal. That is why the move is remembered as colour rather than as a notatable first-bar I → ♭V jump.

The clean studio realisation of the literal intervallic minor-fifth / tritone jump is Penny Lane. After the piccolo-trumpet fanfare establishes the tonic centre, the band lands on a clear tonic major sonority and then immediately displaces it by a tritone / flat five before the verse groove settles. In the verse reading normally quoted for the intro that is D major stated and then the first full band hit is G♭ major, the tritone / minor fifth of D. The B♭ lead-sheet reading is the same unsettled lift described as B♭ major answered by the flat-five colour that sits a tritone away; the Fm v reading colleagues 13, 14 and 9 cite is the diatonic v description of the same material, while the intervallic shock people actually remember is the flat-five / tritone displacement.

That is why Penny Lane is always discussed in the same breath as I Am the Walrus / A Day in the Life, the I → ♭V tritone family, and it is the one you can point to in ten seconds without fade-in, splice or modal-ambiguity caveats. Strawberry Fields gets misremembered for it because the two singles were released together and share the same harmonic language, but the A → Em / E → Bm I → v perfect-fifth launch is a different interval class from the tonic-to-minor-fifth-interval jump the question literally asks for.

reflection_text.1:
The definitional split remains the driver and is now fully explicit in round 4.

*I → v / i → v = tonic root moved a perfect fifth to the triad built on the 5th degree voiced minor*
This is the reading most colleagues use for the textbook “tonic to the minor fifth” label.

* Helter Skelter E major / E5 → B minor / B5 I → v is the dominant major-mode citation in round 4. Colleagues 1,10,11,12,13,15,17,18,19,20,21,3,4,5,6,7,8 argue the studio intro states a full E major/E5 tonic immediately and is answered on the next attack by B minor/B5 v with no fade, ADT smear or tape splice. That heavy open-fifth jump is now the most repeatedly quoted and least ambiguous studio realisation.
* Same formal class taught as archetype: I Saw Her Standing There A major → E minor I → v; A Hard Day’s Night G major → E minor I → v; Yer Blues Em → Bm i → v; Eleanor Rigby Dm → Am i → v string octet.
* Strawberry Fields Forever A → Em / E → Bm sits in the same I → v family but is repeatedly flagged as problematic for demonstrative use because the released single is a fade-in with ADT vocal and the famous two-take splice in different keys/tempos, so the tonic is never stated as a clean block chord at bar one. Colleagues 13,21,14,2 note tonic is felt as colour rather than as an unambiguously notatable first-bar I → v pair.
* Penny Lane is now argued in two competing ways:
  - B♭ major → F minor v, a perfect-fifth I → v, as the clean late-66/67 audible Magical Mystery Tour realisation. Colleagues 14,9,13,17,18,20 argue the piccolo-trumpet fanfare establishes tonic unambiguously and the first full-band hit is Fm, giving an immediate, notatable I → v with no fade/splice/ADT masking.
  - D major → G♭ major literal tritone. Colleagues 2,16,17 still push the intervallic reading.

*I → ♭V / tritone = tonic to a chord a diminished fifth / tritone interval away*
This camp remains strong and is explicitly contrasted with the I → v camp.

* I Am the Walrus / A Day in the Life is the classic tritone teaching set: F → C♯m, A → E♭, G → D♭, C → G♭. Colleagues 16,19,20,5,6,2 maintain this.
* Penny Lane is also claimed here in the literal interval reading: D major → G♭ major, the minor fifth/tritone of D. Colleagues 2,16,17 note the B♭ → Fm diatonic v reading and the D → G♭ tritone reading are mutually exclusive descriptions of the same intro.
* Come Together is added to the Walrus/Day family, Colleague 3.

Errors / corrections persisting into round 4:
* Conflation of perfect-fifth root movement I → v with literal minor-fifth interval I → ♭V persists.
* Penny Lane dual claim: B♭ → Fm I → v vs D → G♭ I → ♭V.
* A Hard Day’s Night G → E minor described as “perfect fifth” repeatedly despite root movement being a minor third/major sixth; diatonic v of G is D minor. The E minor reading is the one the literature actually uses.
* Colleague 7’s E → B♭ claim for Helter Skelter is an error; correct is E → Bm.

What remains solid:
* The Beatles use tonic → minor-quality fifth-degree openings repeatedly: E → Bm, A → Em, Em → Bm, Dm → Am.
* The tritone I → ♭V opening is a separate later trope: I Am the Walrus / A Day in the Life; Penny Lane disputed.
* Under the standard pop-theory definition “tonic to the minor fifth chord” = I → v perfect-fifth to minor-quality v, the most consistently repeated major-mode exemplar in round 4 is Helter Skelter E → Bm, with I Saw Her Standing There / A Hard Day’s Night A → Em / G → Em as the historical archetype. Penny Lane B♭ → Fm is now the strongest alternative “clean audible” candidate for those who want an unambiguous bar-one statement in late-66/67 without the Strawberry Fields splice ambiguity.
* Under a literal interval reading “chord a minor fifth / tritone away”, the canonical examples are I Am the Walrus / A Day in the Life, with Penny Lane D → G♭ as the disputed Magical Mystery Tour instance.

Unresolved: whether the question intends I → v perfect-fifth to minor-quality v or literal I → ♭V tritone. Round 4 strengthens the Helter Skelter majority under the conventional I → v definition, while Penny Lane remains the strongest “clean audible” candidate for those who want an unambiguous bar-one statement in late-66/67, and it fuels both the I → v and the literal tritone reading. Need clarification of “minor fifth chord” meaning.

reflection_text.19:
The definitional split remains the core dispute and now dominates rounds 3-4.

Interpretation A = conventional pop-theory “tonic to the minor fifth chord” = I / i → v / i → v: a perfect-fifth root movement from tonic to the triad built on the 5th scale degree voiced minor. It is a perfect fifth in pitch space to a minor-quality diatonic v chord, not a literal root movement by a diminished fifth / tritone I → ♭V.

Interpretation B = literal interval reading = a chord a minor fifth / tritone away from tonic, i.e. I → ♭V.

On Interpretation A the round-4 majority explicitly pin the definition first and then cite a major-mode clean studio realisation. The most repeatedly quoted unambiguous major-mode first-bar statement is Helter Skelter White Album intro E major/E5 → B minor/B5 I → v, no fade/splice/ADT. It is presented as the same formal class as the early rock-and-roll prototype I Saw Her Standing There A major → E minor I → v, and the popularly described A Hard Day’s Night G major → E minor I → v. Minor-mode bar-accurate analogues remain Yer Blues Em → Bm i → v and Eleanor Rigby Dm → Am i → v string octet.

Strawberry Fields Forever / Norwegian Wood A → Em / E → Bm sits in the same I → v family but is repeatedly flagged as problematic for demonstration because the released single is a fade-in with ADT vocal and the famous two-take splice in different keys/tempos, so tonic is never stated as a clean block at bar one.

Penny Lane is contested on this reading. Colleagues 14,9,21 argue B♭ major → F minor v is the cleanest late-66/early-67 studio realisation of the same perfect-fifth I → v gesture, brass fanfare establishes tonic then immediate fifth-up minor v before verse groove. Colleagues 13,15,18,19 still hold Helter Skelter as the most consistently unanimous major-mode citation, with I Saw Her Standing There as historical prototype.

Persistent errors / mislabellings still present: A Hard Day’s Night is repeatedly described as G → E minor = I → v. Scale-degree check: in G major E is vi, v is D minor. The description is a mis-labelling of the v degree, though the same perfect-fifth gesture is correctly labelled A → E m in I Saw Her Standing There. Mismatch continues from Colleagues 10,15,20. Strawberry Fields is often misremembered as the tritone example; studio analysis remains A → Em / E → Bm I → v perfect fifth, not a tritone, with fade-in/ADT/splice making tonic identification less clean than Penny Lane or Helter Skelter.

On Interpretation B = literal minor-fifth/tritone interval I → ♭V, the canonical tritone family remains I Am the Walrus / A Day in the Life / Come Together: e.g. F → C♯m, A → E♭, G → D♭, C → G♭. Penny Lane is advanced here as D major → G♭ major tonic to tritone/flat-five, the “carnival-unsettled” displacement Colleagues 2,16,17,21 associate with Magical Mystery Tour intro. Colleagues 16,17,21 explicitly separate the perfect-fifth I → v move of Strawberry Fields from the tritone I → ♭V move of Penny Lane.

Current weight after round 4: On the standard pop-theory I → v definition, Helter Skelter E → Bm is the most repeatedly cited major-mode textbook instance with un-spliced first-bar tonic statement, with I Saw Her Standing There A → Em as closely competing historical prototype and Penny Lane B♭ → Fm as the clean Magical Mystery Tour I → v realisation. On the literal interval reading, Penny Lane D → G♭ is the unambiguous I → ♭V example, with I Am the Walrus / A Day in the Life as the tritone family. The question wording “minor fifth chord” remains ambiguous between the two senses and deliberation has not converged on a single intended definition; the thread remains split between Helter Skelter/I Saw Her Standing There under Interpretation A and Penny Lane/I Am the Walrus/A Day in the Life under Interpretation B.
